title: Clothes dryer: safe teardown
summary: An electric clothes dryer gives a 1/3 hp mains motor with its blower wheel, a heating element of about 5 kW, several thermostats and thermal fuses, a long belt and idler, switches and, if fitted, a heavy 240 V cord (many US electric dryers ship without one). Unplug it first; a gas dryer must have its gas turned off and the pipe capped by someone able to do gas work before it moves. Lint inside is very flammable, so clear it before any cutting.

steps.text: Find out whether it is electric or gas before you move it. Look behind it with a torch. An electric dryer has a heavy cord with a big 3- or 4-prong plug (some have no cord, just heavy wires on a terminal block at the back) and no gas pipe. A gas dryer has a gas pipe with a shut-off valve, a flexible connector, and an ordinary 120 V plug.
steps.warn: If you smell gas (rotten eggs), leave at once without touching any switch or plug, or using a phone inside. Air the place from outside.

steps.text: Gas dryer: turn the shut-off valve on the gas pipe to OFF (the handle ends up across the pipe). Then stop. The flexible connector must be undone and the pipe sealed with a proper cap or plug, and leak-tested with soapy water, by someone able to do gas work. If nobody can, leave the dryer where it is and take an electric one instead.
steps.warn: Never pull a gas dryer out on its connector, never leave an open gas pipe, and never improvise a seal with tape or hose. Never test for leaks with a flame.

steps.text: Electric dryer, or a gas dryer once its pipe is capped and its connector undone: pull it out just far enough to reach the outlet and unplug it. A gas dryer runs on 120 V mains, which can also kill. If the cord runs straight into the wall with no plug, switch off its double breaker, lock or tag it, and prove the wires dead with a meter (see safety_mains_isolation). Wait a few minutes before opening it, and longer if it ran lately: the heater duct stays hot.
steps.warn: An electric dryer has 240 V between its two hot wires and 120 V from each to neutral. Either can kill. Prove it dead; don't assume.

steps.text: Move it with a helper onto cardboard with room all round. Pull the vent duct off the back and set it aside.
steps.warn: A full-size dryer can weigh around 57 kg (125 lb). Two people, knees bent, back straight.

steps.text: Clear the lint before anything else. Pull the lint screen, then vacuum or brush the lint out of the screen housing and the vent outlet. Once the panels are off, clear the lint from the cabinet floor and around the heater. Bag it dry.
steps.warn: Lint catches fire very easily. No grinder, torch, cigarette or hot work anywhere near it.

steps.text: Take off the top and front panels: screws at the back edge or under the console, and screws or clips along the front. Front-loading models usually need the console and front panel off first. Photograph every connector before you unplug it. If you find a capacitor, discharge it before touching its terminals (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: Panel edges and the inside of the cabinet are sharp. Wear gloves.

steps.text: Release the belt. Reach under the drum, push the spring-loaded idler pulley against its spring to slacken the belt, and slip the belt off the motor pulley.
steps.warn: The idler spring snaps back when you let go. Keep fingers out from between the pulley and the bracket.

steps.text: Lift the drum out with a helper steadying it; on front-loaders the front bulkhead comes off first. Keep the belt and the drum support rollers. The drum is bulky and its edges are sharp: gloves on, and keep your helper's hands clear.
Heater (electric dryers): it sits in a steel duct at the back or under the drum. Pull its spade terminals, undo its screw or screws, and slide the heater out with its thermostats still attached.
Unscrew the thermostats and the thermal fuse from the heater duct and the blower housing. Tape a label on each saying where it was mounted: they open at different temperatures and some never reset.

Motor and blower: unplug the motor and the belt switch, undo the motor bracket screws, and lift the motor out with the blower wheel. Then take the wheel off the shaft. It may be held by a nut, a set screw or a threaded hub: look for an arrow or marking on the hub before you force it.
Take the door switch, the timer or control board, and the power cord from its terminal block. If you leave the cabinet behind, take its door off.
steps.warn: A child can climb into an abandoned dryer and be trapped. Never leave one with a door on.

steps.text: Test the motor and the heater with your meter before you carry them far (see the testing notes below).

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Drive motor.** A single-phase induction motor of about 1/3 hp; one dryer tech sheet lists a 1/3 hp drive motor (Tech sheet W10042930). It starts through a centrifugal switch on the motor (Tech sheet W10042930), and LG's wiring diagram shows an overload protector in the motor circuit (LG DLE3777W manual). It is a steady workshop motor for a line shaft, grinder, pump or saw wherever mains power exists. Read the motor's own label for its voltage before you power it; don't assume 240 V because the dryer was 240 V (skill_read_nameplate).
- **Blower wheel.** With the motor it makes a strong blower for a forge (build_brake_drum_forge), shelter ventilation or a drying cabinet.
- **Heating element.** The Samsung DV45H electric models list a 5,300 W heater (Samsung DV45H manual). LG's electric heater reads 10 Ω from its common terminal to each of the other two terminals, and 20 Ω between those two (LG DLE3777W manual). Power falls with the square of voltage, so the same element on 120 V gives only about a quarter: roughly 1.3 kW. If the coil is bare wire, treat it as live at mains voltage. Use it to heat air only, inside an earthed metal duct nobody can reach into, with a fan, a fuse or breaker, and an over-heat cut-out. Keep lint and dust away from it and never leave it running unattended. Never put a bare coil in water.
- **Thermostats and thermal fuses.** Snap-action safety switches. In the LG DLE3777W the thermal cut-off opens at about 130 °C (266 °F) and does not reset; the high-limit thermostat opens at about 125 °C (257 °F) and closes at 105 °C (221 °F); the outlet thermostat opens at about 85 °C (185 °F) and closes at 65 °C (149 °F) (LG DLE3777W manual). Another dryer's thermal fuse opens at 91 °C (196 °F) (Tech sheet W10042930). Read the temperature stamped on each one and test it for continuity before you trust it; a thermal fuse that has opened is spent, and one whose rating you can't read is not a safe cut-out. Use them as over-heat cut-outs on a heater, oven or dryer you build.
- **Belt and idler.** A long ribbed belt and a spring-loaded idler pulley: a ready-made tensioner for belt drives.
- **Switches.** The door switch has common, normally-open and normally-closed terminals (LG DLE3777W manual). LG's idler switch sits on the motor bracket and its lever is worked by the drum belt (LG DLE3777W manual).
- **Power cord.** A heavy cord for a dryer circuit: Samsung's manual calls for a cord kit rated at least 120/240 V and 30 A with three No. 10 copper conductors, and says never to reuse an old dryer's cord on a dryer (Samsung DV45H manual). Good heavy cable for leads carrying up to about 30 A once you have checked the insulation for cracks and heat damage.
- **Drum and rollers.** A large sheet-steel cylinder for storage or a compost sieve, and rollers that are small wheels on axles.
- **Lint.** Lint burns very easily (USFA dryer fires). Bagged dry, it is useful tinder (skill_fire_starting).

## Testing what you got out

- **Motor:** with the motor unplugged, one tech sheet gives about 2.4–3.6 Ω across the main winding and 2.4–3.8 Ω across the start winding (Tech sheet W10042930). An open reading means a broken winding (see test_motor).
- **Heater:** LG's electric heater reads 10 Ω from its common terminal to each other terminal and 20 Ω between those two (LG DLE3777W manual). Others differ: work out what yours should read from its label (ohms = volts x volts / watts), and treat an open reading as a broken coil.
- **Thermostats:** LG lists under 5 Ω for its hi-limit and outlet thermostats when cool and an open reading as failed (LG DLE3777W manual). A thermal cut-off that reads open has blown for good.
- **Door switch:** common to NC reads under 1 Ω with the plunger out; pushed in, common to NO closes instead (LG DLE3777W manual).

## Variations

- **Electric dryers** in the US mostly need 120/240 V, 60 Hz service with 30 A protection on both lines, wired 3-wire or 4-wire; some need 120/208 V service (Samsung DV45H manual).
- **Gas dryers** run on 120 V, 15 A and have a burner, gas valve and igniter in place of the element; the Samsung DV45H gas burner is rated 22,000 BTU/h (Samsung DV45H manual). GE's installation instructions require a qualified installer, a new connector every time (never the old flexible one), and a soapy-water leak test, never a flame (GE gas dryer install). Take the gas valve and igniter only after the pipe has been capped, and never put a salvaged gas valve back on a gas line.
- **Heaters** differ: one tech sheet's wiring diagram shows a 5,400 W heater made of two 2,700 W legs (Tech sheet W10042930), and LG's electric heater has a common terminal and two ends (LG DLE3777W manual).
- **Newer dryers** have thermistors, moisture-sensing strips in the drum and an electronic control (Tech sheet W10042930; LG DLE3777W manual), and some Samsung steam models connect to a cold water tap (Samsung DV45H manual).
- **Commercial and coin-op dryers** are bigger and often three-phase: see teardown_commercial_laundry.
- **Heat-pump dryers** recirculate their air in a closed loop, use a refrigerant to take the moisture out, and need no vent (ENERGY STAR heat pump dryer). Treat that loop like a fridge: leave it sealed (safety_refrigerant).

## Lint and fire

In 2008–2010 about 2,900 dryer fires a year were reported in US residential buildings. Failure to clean was the leading factor (34 percent), and dust, fibre and lint were the items most often ignited first (USFA dryer fires). A dryer that has stood for months can still be packed with lint. Clear it before you cut, grind or solder anything nearby.

## What to leave

- The thin painted cabinet panels and plastic parts, unless you need sheet.
- Lint-packed ducts and vent hose.
- Every gas part of a gas dryer whose pipe has not been capped.
- Thermistors and moisture strips: small value.
